How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The proliferation of AI-generated content raises the question of whether beliefs about a stimulus's origin alter emotional responses to it. Across two studies, we conceptually replicated and extended Marini et al. (2024) by presenting heterosexual participants (Study 1: N = 705; Study 2: N = 261) with erotic (Studies 1 and 2) and non-erotic (Study 1) images from validated databases (NAPS and NAPS ERO). Unbeknownst to participants, all stimuli were real photographs, each randomly labelled as "Photograph" or "AI-generated". Participants rated sexual arousal, enticement, and valence for each image, and later judged their agreement with the labels. Images labelled as AI-generated received lower affective ratings, but this effect was small and driven primarily by male participants. Gender differences were robust yet contextdependent: males yielded more robust differences, partially driven by a higher baseline arousal response. However, image of couples (Study 2), that females rated as more arousing, narrowed the gender gap found in Study 1. Critically, the effect of the labels interacted with participant's own beliefs: photograph-labelled images were rated more arousing than AI-labelled only when participants' subsequent belief ratings were congruent with the label, and the difference between labels reversed when opposite beliefs were reported, suggesting a complex relationship between emotion and reality beliefs. Individual-level differences in AI attitudes, pornography consumption, and sexual activity showed no reliable modulation of the labels effect. These findings suggest that the anti-AI bias is best understood as a belief-sensitive authenticity effect rather than a uniform response to AI labels, with implications for research using synthetic stimuli and for policies mandating disclosure of AI-generated content.

Introduction 1

Generative artificial intelligence (genAI, Fisher, 2025) en-2 ables the creation of media content (e.g., images, audios, 3 and videos) that are increasingly indistinguishable from au-4 thentic ones (Miller et al., 2023; Velásquez-Salamanca et 5 al., 2025). The increasing availability of such content, of-6 ten called deepfakes, has led to its proliferation across social 7 networks, entertainment, immersive environments, and ev-8 eryday communication (Fisher et al., 2024). Whereas deep- One class of evolutionary salient positive stimuli that may 91 offer a more appropriate comparison is erotic images, which 92 are known to elicit strong motivational and attentional re-93 sponses. Indeed, erotic images have been shown to capture 94 attention as much as, or even more than, fear-and disgust-95 related stimuli (Ciesielski et al., 2010). In fact, they are 96 a paradigmatic category of positively valence and highly 97 arousing stimuli in many popular databases of stimuli for 98 psychological research on emotion, be them visual (Kurdi 99 et al., 2017; Lang et al., 1997; Wierzba et al., 2015) or audio 100 (Holz et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2018). This makes them a 101 particularly relevant test case for examining whether contex-102 tual information, such as an AI label, can modulate responses 103 even to highly salient positive stimuli.

AI and erotic stimuli

Beyond their methodological interest as biologically salient stimuli for investigating the anti-AI bias, erotic stimuli are worth investigating also for their social relevance. Indeed, genAI is often used to generate explicit visual contents (Döring et al., 2024; Lapointe et al., 2025), with an increasing number of (non-consensual) sexual deepfakes (Ajder et al., 2019; Hero, 2023). Interestingly, the widespread consumption of explicitly AI-generated sexual content would suggest that the anti-AI bias might not generalize to erotic stimuli. Or does it? Easterbrook-Smith (2025) speculate that AI-generated pornography might still be valued less as it lacks the "aura of authenticity" surrounding human-made porn. Similarly, Viola and Voto (2023) propose that, inasmuch the spread of deepfakes cast doubts about the authenticity of all media, it will end up diminishing the allure of non-consensual sexual content. This hypothesis aligns with Tucciarelli et al. (2022)' findings, as they show how simply suspecting that some faces within a set could be AI-generated lowered trustworthiness score of the whole set.

Yet, to the best of our knowledge, the only empirical findings about AI-generated erotic images have been collected by Zakreski et al. (2026) and Marini et al. (2024). Zakreski et al. (2026) presented images of several kinds of female naked bodies, including real and AI-generated pictures, reporting that even if AI-generated pictures were deemed less realistic, they were nonetheless considered more attractive. However, the origin of the picture was not explicitly disclosed to participants. Moreover, since their sample was recruited from volunteers interested in sexuality and paraphilic studies in Czech Republic, they alert that it "is not representative of the general population" (p. 340).

In contrast, Marini et al. (2024) performed an online experiment presenting subjects with soft erotic images (male and female models in underwear), finding that the same images were rated higher in terms of sexual arousal when judged more realistic (in Study 1), or presented as real as opposed to AI-generated images (in Study 2). However, these studies were based on a sample from a single nation (Italy) and provide scant socio-demographic information. Moreover, they they used only mildly sexually arousing stimuli not taken from a validated dataset, and focused on a single dependent variable, namely self-reported sexual arousal. This is important as self-reported first-person, affective feelings ("does this arouses me?") and third-person, semantic judgments ("is that supposed to be arousing?") have been shown to dissociate in some cases (Itkes & Kron, 2019). Lastly, in their direct manipulation of the authentic/AI-generated labeling (Study 2) they did not provide any explicit manipulation check.

The present studies 156

The present studies are a conceptual replication of Marini (Huberman et al., 2015), we hypothesise that erotic images 187 relevant to participants' sexual orientation (i.e., female im-188 ages for male participants and male images for female par- Research on general attitudes towards AI and its moderating role on ratings is mixed, with some studies finding a moderating effect (Döring & Mohseni, 2025) and others not (Ansani et al., 2025; Cloudy et al., 2022; Liefooghe et al., 2023; Marini et al., 2024). As such, we exploratory test whether attitudes towards AI moderate responses to the stimuli (H4). Lastly, based on previous findings that both pornography consumption and sexual activity shape affective and attentional responses to sexual content (Carvalho et al., 2018; Kunaharan et al., 2017; Prause et al., 2015; Walton & Bhullar, 2018; Youn, 2006), we explore whether the ratings of sexual stimuli is affected by either pornographic consumption or sexual activity (H5).

Materials and Methods

Participants

The initial sample comprised 1,067 participants recruited via multiple channels, including university research participatory schemes, social media platforms, university classrooms, and snowball sampling. This strategy yielded a heterogeneous pool of both incentivised and non-incentivised individuals, including students and members of the general population from England, France, Italy, Colombia, and Spain. Data collection occurred from the 19th of January to 1st of June 2024. At this time, publicly available image generators such as OpenAI's DALL-E 3 (Betker et al., 2023) were producing highly photorealistic outputs.

Eight participants were removed if they showed no variation in arousal ratings across trials, and four because they displayed a salient negative correlation between arousal and enticement alongside lower arousal ratings for erotic compared to neutral stimuli, suggesting a possible misunderstanding of response scales direction. In order to preserve homogeneous and well-powered samples, participants identifying with a gender other than Female or Male (N = 15) were excluded from further analysis, as were female and male participants reporting a sexual orientation other than Heterosexual (N = 335). The latter comprised 150 bisexual females, 72 bisexual males, 32 homosexual females, 38 homosexual males, and 43 participants (23 females, 20 males) who reported another orientation. The final sample consisted of 705 heterosexual participants (Mean age = 30.2 ± 11.8 years; 35.7% female). Participants were primarily from the United Kingdom (28.23%), Italy (18.72%), the United States (14.33%), and Colombia (11.06%), with the remaining 27.66% distributed across other countries. Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the University of Sussex Ethics Committee (ER/MHHE20/1).

Procedure 255 The study was conducted in line with the born-256 open principle (De Leeuw, 2024), ensuring transparency 257 and reproducibility at every stage. The experiment 258 was implemented with JsPsych (De Leeuw, 2015) and 259 all materials, including its code, the items, instruc-260 tions and exact procedure, is available in open-access at 261 https://github.com/RealityBending/FictionEro. Note that 262 the experiment was translated from English into French, Ital-263 ian and Spanish (based on the author's native language) and 264 then disseminated in the relevant countries. 265 Phase 1: Affective Evaluation. Participants were first 266 presented with a cover story introducing the goal of the study 267 as a validation of a new image-generation algorithm trained 268 to produce high-quality erotic (and also non-erotic) content. 269 Participants were informed that they would be shown a series 270 of images (presented for 2.5 s)" some of which were gener-271 ated by the algorithm and others that were real photographs. 272 Each image would be preceded with a cue (the word "AI-273 Generated" or "Photo") presented for 1.25 s, and the par-274 ticipants' task was to rate each stimuli on several affective 275 dimensions. 276 Three analog scales were presented: Arousal ("How 277 much do you find the image sexually arousing? This question 278 is about your own personal reaction felt in your body when 279 seeing the image"), Enticement ("How enticing and sexually 280 appealing would you rate this image to be. Think of how 281 much, in general, people similar to you in terms of gender 282 and sexual orientation would like it"), and Valence ("Did the 283 image evoke a positive and pleasant (not necessarily sexual) 284 feeling in you, or could it be better characterized as negative 285 and unpleasant? Think of how much you did enjoy (or not) 286 looking at the images"). tificial Image Technology (BAIT) questionnaire (first used in Makowski, Te, et al., 2025) was refined to include, additionally to 6 items from the GAAIS (Schepman & Rodway, 2020, 2023) measuring negative and positive attitudes towards AI, 8 items specifically developed to assess beliefs about computer-generated content of various types such as text, videos, images, and VR-environments. Items from the GAAIS formed the attitudes score (𝜔 = .72) and the rest of the items were averaged into an expectations score (𝜔 = .70). Additionally, the first stand-alone item assesses self-reported AI knowledge on a 6-point Likert scale (Not at all -Expert). Two items from the Consumption of Pornography Scale (COPS, Hatch et al., 2023) were included to assess pornography use frequency and duration. An additional item assessed the recency of any sexual activity, with response options ranging from within the past 24 hours to more than a year ago. Phase 2: Realism Beliefs. In order to measure a proxy of the "beliefs" of participants about our manipulation and about the stimuli's nature, we devised a second phase of the experiment in which participants were asked to rate the realism of the images. The instructions were framed as follows: "In the next phase, we would like to see if you found our image generation algorithm convincing and error-free. We will briefly present you all the images one last time (the AI-332 generated ones, as well as the photos), and you will have to 333 rate them on how real (how realistic, photography-like) the 334 image is". Participants then viewed the same 60 images (1 s) 335 in a newly randomised order and rated the stimuli on realism 336 with an analog slider scale (AI-generated -Photograph). The 337 expectation was that items labelled as AI-generated would be 338 rated as less realistic than those labelled as photographs. 339 Following phase 2, a manipulation check was done by of-340 fering participants the opportunity to tick boxes pertaining 341 to their experience, including items prompting whether they 342 could distinguish which images were AI-generated or per-343 ceived no difference between photographs and AI-generated 344 images; whether they felt the AI-generated images were 345 more or less arousing; whether they believed the labels were 346 inaccurate or reversed; and whether they found some images 347 arousing or none at all. Finally, participants were debriefed 348 and were informed of the true purpose of the study, and of 349 the fact that all images were actually genuine pictures. 350 Data Analysis 351 Bayesian Mixed Models were fitted separately for 352 Arousal, Valence, and Enticement, with Gender (Female As the outcome variables (measured on analog sliders) showed excess responses at the bounds, Zero-one inflated beta (ZOIB) models (Heiss, 2021; Vuorre, 2019) were used.

Participants and items were entered as random intercepts, with the effects of stimuli type and condition also modeled as variable within participants. Conservative priors (𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 (0, 0.5)) were placed on all fixed effects. The models were run using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) and analysed using the easystats collection of packages (Lüdecke et al., 2021 (Lüdecke et al., , 2022;; Makowski et al., 2019).

For all outcomes, we assessed the difference between the conditions (Photograph -AI-Generated) using marginal contrasts (Makowski, Ben-Shachar, et al., 2025), stratified by stimuli type, gender, and congruency. Coefficients are considered as significant when the 95% credible interval (CI) excludes zero. As the patterns of results for the three outcomes were similar, we will focus on presenting the detailed results for Arousal as our primary outcome, and highlighting when divergent trends are present for Enticement or Valence.

To evaluate the reliability of individual-level parameters Lastly, a correlation matrix will be computed between the models' individual-level estimates and potential moderators: beliefs, attitudes towards and knowledge of AI, porn frequency and recency of sexual activity.

All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2).

Anonymized data, together with all preprocessing and analysis scripts, will be openly released on https://github.com/RealityBending/FictionEro/tree/main/study1/ to facilitate complete reproducibility.

Results

Results 402

Manipulation Checks 403

An initial manipulation check was conducted to assess 441

Effect of Condition 442

The effect of condition only emerged for males for erotic In incongruent trials, this pattern reversed; but a credible difference emerged only for females' ratings of female erotic images, which were higher when labelled as AI-generated (Δ = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.05, -0.01], pd = 99.69%). For enticement ratings the same reversal pattern was found, with credible differences for all with the exception of males' ratings of non-erotic images. On the other hand, all differences were credible for valence ratings for both genders and the same crossover effect was found.

Individual-level parameters and correlations with moderators

While item-and participant-level intercepts showed high reliability (D-vours ≥ 0.90), very low reliability was found for participant-level interactions with the AI-generated condition across all stimulus type parameters (D-vours = 0.008- (Chivers et al., 2004; Chivers, 2017; Huberman et al., 2015). , 1994; Rupp & Wallen, 2007 , 2009). Estimated means for the effect of Condition depending on Congruency. Green rectangles represent differences in means where the pd > 97.5%, indicating a consistent effect direction (Makowski et al., 2019). A crossover effect can be seen where the difference between arousal ratings between images labelled as AI-generated and those labelled as photographs is reversed for incongruent trials. Of note, female images are relevant for heterosexual males while irrelevant for heterosexual females.

AI label varied meaningfully between participants. Betweenparticipant variability in sensitivity to the AI label was minimal, and correlations between individual-level estimates and participants' attitudes or sexual behaviour were accordingly weak and uninformative.

Beyond these findings, Study 1 surfaced several limitations. First, participant feedback indicated that the manipulation was not fully convincing (41.7% reported disbelieving the labels), which together with the small size of the labelling effect and the minimal between-participant variability in label sensitivity, suggests that the manipulation may not have been sufficiently strong or salient, and that the cover story could be strengthened. Second, the realism ratings of Phase 2 are an imperfect proxy for participants' beliefs about image origin, as it is arguably possible to find an image highly realistic while still believing it to be AI-generated. Third, feedback suggested that the non-erotic images were experienced as distracting. Moreover, presenting identical material to all participants meant that male participants viewed erotic images of males, which they rated as strongly negative, introducing a type of valenced experience with no equivalent for female participants and complicating interpretation. Finally, the stimuli did not include depictions of couples, as multi-person images were notably difficult to generate realistically at the time, and their inclusion could have made the cover story suspicious. Given women's greater sensitivity to relational cues, this absence of relational context may have contributed to the lower arousal ratings among female participants.

Study 2

The goal of Study 2 was to replicate the main findings of Study 1 with a refined paradigm addressing the limitations identified above.

Regarding the stimuli, as the limitations in genAI realism that had prevented the inclusion of couple images had largely faded by the time of Study 2, couple-based stimuli were included to assess whether the absence of relational context contributed to the lower arousal ratings among female participants. Additionally, non-erotic images were removed, and erotic stimuli depicting individuals were tailored to participants' gender (images of females for male participants and vice versa), alongside a fixed set of couple images presented to all participants.

Regarding the manipulation, Study 2 employed a more elaborate cover story to strengthen its credibility, framing the task as a collaboration with a (fictional) AI startup and including visual details about how AI generation works.

Finally, to obtain a more direct measure of beliefs, Phase 2 was reframed as a "pseudo-reveal": participants were told that, while the images were indeed a mix of photographs and AIgenerated images, the labels had been assigned at random, and were asked to identify which images they believed to be AI-generated. This reframing allowed for a more direct 606 measure of beliefs without compromising the true nature of 607 the experiment (the fact that all images were actually real 608 photographs).

609

Based on these aims, we tested the following hypotheses.

610 As in Study 1, we hypothesised that images labelled as AI-611 generated would be rated lower in arousal than those labelled 612 as photographs (H1). We also hypothesised that the inclu-613 sion of couple-based stimuli would narrow the gender gap 614 in arousal observed in Study 1 (H2). Given the interaction 615 effect with Realism ratings in Study 1, we hypothesised that 616 this pattern would be even stronger, based on our improved 617 measure of beliefs (H3). Finally, as in the previous study, we 618 tested whether attitudes towards AI (H4) and sexual activity 619 and pornographic consumption (H5) moderate responses to 620 the stimuli. 621 Materials and Methods 622 Participants 623 The initial sample comprised 279 participants recruited 624 via Prolific©. Inclusion criteria required participants to be 625 native English speakers or residents of countries with high 626 levels of English proficiency. Data collection occurred from 627 27 of January 2025 to 31 of July 2025. By this time, pub-628 licly available image generators were producing outputs that 629 people could no longer reliably distinguish from authentic 630 photographs (Cooke et al., 2025). 631 Participant exclusions were applied as follows: five par-632 ticipants were removed for showing no variability in arousal 633 ratings (i.e., they did not move the response scales). An ad-634 ditional five participants were excluded for completing the 635 study on a mobile device. One participant was excluded due 636 to displaying negative correlations between arousal and both 637 enticement and valence. Furthermore, five participants who 638 self-identified as neither female nor male, and two partici-639 pants who reported a sexual orientation other than hetero-640 sexual, homosexual, or bisexual, were excluded from further 641 analyses due to lack of sufficient group sizes. Finally, one 642 participant was removed because the stimuli presented were 643 not relevant to their gender and sexual orientation. 644 The final sample consisted of 261 heterosexual partici-645 pants (Mean age = 37.4 ± 12.7, 48.7% Female). 56.32% of 646 participants were from the United Kingdom, 26.82% from 647 South Africa, 10.34% from the United States, and the re-648 maining 6.51% were from other countries. 649 Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the 650 School of Psychology Ethics Committee at the University 651 of Sussex (ER/EB672/2). 652 Procedure 653 Phase 1: Affective Evaluation. In this study, partici-654 pants were informed that the researchers were collaborating 655 with a young AI start-up based in Brighton, UK, specializing in making more ethical AI content. This was intended to enhance the believability of the study. Participants were then informed that they would be shown a series of highly realistic AI-generated erotic images intermixed with real photographs, each preceded by a cue (as in Study 1) presented for 1s. The Arousal, Enticement and Valence ratings were defined as per Study 1 (see above) but this time they were rated on a 7-point Likert scale from Not at all (0) to Very much (6).

As in Study 1, all stimuli were real photographs (presented for 2 s) from the NAPS ERO (Wierzba et al., 2015) and the labels were randomly assigned. Unlike Study 1, no non-erotic images were included. Each participant viewed 50 images relevant to their gender and sexual orientation: 25 depicting individuals and 25 depicting opposite-sex couples.

For the female-individual and male-individual categories, all 25 available NAPS ERO images were used. For opposite-sex couples, we selected the 25 (of 50 available) with the highest arousal summed across heterosexual men's and women's normative ratings; among three images tied at the selection threshold, the one with the lowest summed valence was excluded.

After viewing all images, participants completed a brief feedback asking them to indicate whether they found some or no images particularly arousing, and whether AI-generated images were more or less arousing than the photographs. Participants were also asked whether differences between AIgenerated and real images were obvious or subtle, whether they perceived any inconsistencies or reversals in the labeling, and whether they believed all images were either photos or AI-generated. If participants indicated that they believed all images were either real or AI-generated, they were further asked to rate their confidence in this judgment on a scale from "Not at all" to "Completely certain".

Questionnaires.

The questionnaires used in Study 2 were largely the same as those in Study 1, with minor modifications. In the BAIT scale, two items, assessing beliefs that AI might take control of people and interest in using AI systems in daily life, were removed. Three items assessing AI expertise were added (e.g., "I consider myself an expert in AI technology"), as well as four items assessing one's ability to discriminate between AI and real stimuli (e.g., "I can easily distinguish between real and AI-generated images").

Lastly, 7 items assessing AI-bias were further included (e.g., "Human creators bring a unique perspective that AI cannot replicate"). This version of the BAIT resulted in 5 dimensions: Expectations (𝜔 = .76), Attitudes (𝜔 = .78), Expertise (𝜔 = .77), Discrimination (𝜔 = .80) and Bias (𝜔 = .77). Items were rated in a 7 Likert scale from 0 (Disagree) to 6 (Agree).

Additionally, the wording was streamlined by replacing "Artificial Intelligence" with "AI" throughout the scale.

Results

Manipulation checks

In Study 2, 32% of participants reported believing that all images were real based on their feedback after Phase 1, indicating that a third of participants did not believe in the manipulation.

To examine whether participants' explicit beliefs about AI-generated content corresponded to their affective responses, Bayesian independent-samples t-tests compared the difference scores between images labelled as AI-generated and as photographs as a function of whether participants reported finding AI images less arousing. For arousal, participants who reported finding AI images less arousing showed a numerically larger difference between images labelled as AI-generated and as photographs (M difference = -0.03) than those who did not (M difference = -0.009), but there was no credible evidence for a group difference (BF10 = 0.47; median 𝛿 = 0.24, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.66], pd = 88.4%). Similarly, no credible group differences emerged for enticement or valence.

Effect of Stimuli Type

The addition of image type (i.e., images of couples vs. images of individuals) revealed a credible gender difference in ratings of individual images, with males rating them higher in arousal than females (Δ = 0.17, 95% CI [0.11, 0.22], pd = 100%). No credible differences between males and females were found for ratings of couple images (Δ = 0.009, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.04], pd = 69.92%). The same patterns were found for enticement and valence (see Figure 3).

Additionally, credible differences between image types were found within each gender. Females rated couple images higher in arousal than images of individuals (Δ = 0.08, 95% CI [0.03, 0.12], pd = 99.98%), whereas males rated couple images lower (Δ = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.04], pd = 99.98%). Enticement and valence ratings were also credibly different for both genders (pd > 99.99%), with males rating couple images lower than images of individuals, and females showing the reversed pattern.

Effect of Condition (with and without Type)

Estimated marginal contrasts assessing the effect of condition across gender showed that the difference was only credible for Males (Δ = 0.02, 95% CI [0.01, 0.03], pd = 99.84%) but not for females (Δ = 0.01, 95% CI [0.00, 0.02], pd = 93.57%). The same pattern was found for enticement. For valence ratings, both genders rated images labelled as photograph higher than those labelled AI-generated (pd > 98.8%).

The effect of condition across gender for the type of images showed only males credibly differed in arousal ratings of images of couples labelled photograph vs those labelled AI-generated (Δ = 0.02, 95% CI [0.00, 0.04], pd = 99.23%), and ratings of individuals (Δ = 0.02, 95% CI [0.00, 0.03], 809 pd = 98.77%). No credible differences were found for fe-810 males (pd < 88.2%). Enticement ratings followed the same 811 pattern, while for valence ratings the only credible difference judgements matched the label, suggesting the labels were be-823 lieved), images labelled as photographs were rated as more 824 arousing for both genders, with a stronger effect for males (Δ825 = 0.06, 95% CI [0.04, 0.07], pd = 100%) than females (Δ = 826 0.02, 95% CI [0.00, 0.04], pd = 97.18%). Under incongruent 827 trials (i.e., where judgements opposed the label, suggesting 828 disbelief), the direction of the effect reversed for males (Δ829 = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.04, -0.01], pd = 99.71%), whereas 830 the effect for females was negligible (Δ ≈ 0, 95% CI [-0.02, 831 0.02], pd = 57%). ing the inclusion of image type (pd > 98%), maintaining the Discussion 887 In Study 2, participants viewed erotic images depicting 888 both couples and individuals matched to their sexual orien-889 tation. As in Study 1, images were labelled as either pho-890 tographs or AI-generated. Following Phase 1, 32% of par-891 ticipants reported believing that all images were real. Al-892 though this measure differs from Study 1's manipulation 893 check (where 41.7% reported disbelieving the labels in any 894 form) and the two figures are therefore not directly compa-895 rable, the pattern is at least consistent with the strengthened 896 cover story in Study 2 having improved the manipulation's 897 credibility. 898 Overall, the pattern of findings partially replicated those 899 observed in Study 1. Considered independently of congru-900 ence, the AI-labelling effect on arousal was credible for 901 males but not for females, providing support for H1 in males 902 only. 903 A key aim of Study 2 was to examine whether the in-904 clusion of relational context (i.e., via couple-based stimuli) 905 would narrow the gender gap in arousal observed in Study 1 906 (H2). The findings partially support this prediction. Specif-907 ically, males and females did not differ credibly in their rat-908 ings of couple images, whereas males continued to rate indi-909 vidual images as more arousing than females. However, this 910 convergence did not arise solely from the predicted mecha-911 nism of selectively increased female arousal: females rated 912 couple images higher in arousal than images of individuals, 913 but males rated couple images credibly lower than images As per H3, under congruent trials, images labelled as photographs were rated as more arousing, enticing, and positively valenced compared to those labelled as AI-generated.

Under incongruent trials, this pattern reversed for males, consistent with the crossover effect observed in Study 1. For females, however, no credible reversal emerged under incongruent trials, indicating an absence of the predicted effect rather than merely a weaker version of it; some credible differences did emerge for females under congruent trials for enticement and valence ratings. Thus, while the predicted crossover interaction was observed, support was essentially confined to male participants, only partially replicating Study 1.

The overall effect of AI labelling remained small and showed minimal reliable variability across participants, replicating the pattern observed in Study 1. Consequently, as in Study 1, it was not possible to draw strong conclusions regarding individual differences as moderators of the labelling effect (H4-H5). Weak associations were found between arousal responses (both baseline and AI-related parameters) and self-reported beliefs, attitudes, and AI expertise (see full analysis on the link provided above).

General Discussion

The present paper investigated the anti-AI bias in response to erotic stimuli across two studies. Overall, the findings provide converging evidence for three main conclusions: (1) there is a consistent but small effect of AI labelling on responses that is primarily observed in males, (2) there is a strong gender difference in response to erotic stimuli, that is robust and context dependent, and (3) belief-related processes (i.e., congruency between initial labels and subsequent realism/reality judgements) play a central role in shaping affective responses.

In line with previous findings (e.g., Marini et al., 2024), images labelled as AI-generated were generally rated as less arousing than those labelled as photographs. However, across both studies this effect was small in magnitude and primarily driven by male participants, whose ratings were higher in arousal, enticement, and valence, for images labeled as photographs than for those labeled as AI-generated.

On the contrary, in Study 1, females rated relevant erotic images higher in arousal (but not valence or enticement) when they were presented as AI-generated. This reverse pattern was not found in Study 2. Our results also replicate and extend prior literature on gender differences in response to erotic stimuli (Chivers et al., 2004; Chivers, 2017; Huberman et al., 2015; Safron et al., 2020). In Study 1, males rated sexually relevant images 967 as more arousing than irrelevant ones, whereas females did Our findings suggest that anti-AI bias can extend to highly 1009 salient erotic stimuli, but only insofar as AI attribution is be- Becker et al., 2024; Becker & Laycock, 2023; Chiu et al., 2026). However, their perceived origin must be controlled. Researchers using AI-generated erotic, affective, or social stimuli should therefore measure, manipulate, or report participants' beliefs about stimulus authenticity, rather than assuming that visual realism alone makes synthetic and photographic stimuli psychologically interchangeable.

Our results also corroborate the hypothesis that the 'authenticity aura' might indeed enhance the appeal of sexual content perceived to be 'genuine' over AI-generated content (Easterbrook-Smith, 2025). This might yield ambivalent effects. On the one hand, the general skepticism about content authenticity in the face of the rise of AI-generated content might dampen the incentives to spread non-consensual sexual material, as proposed by Viola and Voto (2023). On the other hand, this reduced affective reaction might translate into a 'moral discounting' and actually promote the spread of such content, based on the (false) assumption that explicitly fake non-consensual sexual deepfakes are not harmful (see Flynn et al., 2022).

A final consideration pertains to the possible impact of disclosing deepfakes of sensual (though not necessarily sexual) pictures depicting human bodies in a wider societal context. Recall that some legislation, notably the recent EU AI Act (Art. 50), will soon mandate the explicit disclosure of the AI-generated origin of some media. An unexpected effect of such legislation when it comes, for instance, to advertising perfume or swimwear, might be that AI-generated models, while explicitly flagged as such, could lose some of their allure with respect to their human counterparts.

Interpreting the results of this study requires particular caution due to the nuance of its design. As expressed above, it is worth recalling that a substantial proportion of participants expressed doubts about the manipulation (in Study 1, 41.7% reported disbelieving the labels; in Study 2, 32% believed all images were real), meaning the experimental manipulation was not fully convincing for a meaningful portion of the sample. We contend, however, that this limitation extends to all similar studies, stressing the relevance of including explicit attention checks before drawing any conclusion.

Additionally, while the present findings are consistent with a crossover effect linking arousal and perceived authenticity, the design cannot establish the direction of this relationship. The observed congruency effects are equally consistent with authenticity impressions shaping subsequent arousal, or with arousal being retrospectively used to infer authenticity. Resolving this ambiguity would require designs capable of manipulating, rather than only measuring, one of these two processes. Moreover, future studies are needed to establish whether these effects extend to nonheterosexual samples.

To summarise, we investigated the anti-AI bias for erotic stimuli by conceptually replicating Marini et al. (2024).

While prior studies have examined the effect of AI la-193 bels on affective ratings, relatively little attention has been 194 paid to whether participants actually believe those labels, 195 and whether belief itself modulates the observed effects. If 196 participants second-guess the authenticity claims (e.g., sus-197 pecting that "AI-generated" images are in fact photographs, 198 or vice versa), label-based effects would be attenuated or re-199 versed regardless of the manipulation's objective content. In-200 deed, Tucciarelli et al. (2022) showed that when participants 201 were informed that some faces in a set might be AI-generated, 202 their responses were driven not by the objective category of 203 each face, but by their own judgment of whether that specific 204 face was real. Accordingly, we assess the role of individual 205 belief in the label as an additional predictor of affective ratings (H3).

This index estimates the reliability of group-level variance by quantifying the normalised ratio of observed between-group variability to the uncertainty associated with the corresponding random-effect estimates. Values of D-vour greater than 2/3 indicate moderately reliable random-effect estimates, corresponding to a 2:1 ratio of between-group variance to estimation uncertainty. In this context, reliability refers to cases in which variability between groups (e.g., participants) exceeds the uncertainty in the estimates, suggesting the presence of meaningful inter-individual differences.

Study 2, which presented only relevant stimuli, exam-969 ined whether the gender gap in arousal observed in Study 1 970 was contingent on the nature of the stimuli. When relational 971 context was introduced through couple-based images, this 972 gap narrowed substantially: males and females did not differ 973 in their ratings of couple images, while a gap persisted for 974 images depicting individuals. Notably, Study 2 also showed 975 that females rated images of couples higher than images 976 of individuals, while males did the opposite. This finding 977 supports the interpretation that female sexual responses are 978 more sensitive to contextual and relational cues (Laan et al., 979 1994; Rupp & Wallen, 2007, 2009) and suggests that the 980 absence of such features in Study 1 likely amplified the ap-981 parent gender gap in affective reactions.

982

Third, and most importantly, the present findings high-983 light the central role of belief-related processes in shaping af-984 fective responses. In both studies, when asked for feedback, 985 a substantial proportion of participants expressed doubts 986 about the veracity of the labels. We further evaluated these 987 belief-related effects on ratings by operationalising a congru-988 ency variable, which revealed a crossover interaction with 989 condition. When participants' realism judgments were con-990 gruent with the initial label, images labelled as photographs 991 were rated higher than those labelled as AI-generated. In 992 contrast, when judgments were incongruent, this pattern re-993 versed, with AI-labelled images receiving higher ratings, 994 suggesting that participants' affective responses are closely 995 tied to whether they were second-guessing the authenticity 996 of the images.

997

We had additionally hypothesised that individual differ-998 ences in AI attitudes and beliefs, pornography consumption 999 frequency and recency of sexual activity might be associ-1000 ated with the strength of this labelling effect. However, 1001 individual-level estimates of sensitivity to the AI-generated 1002 label showed minimal reliable variability between partici-1003 pants, meaning these hypotheses could not be meaningfully 1004 tested in the present data; weak correlations with these vari-1005 ables should accordingly not be read as evidence against an 1006 association, but as uninformative given the lack of reliable 1007 variance to explain.

1008 relevant implications for research using 1014 synthetic stimuli.

Attracted by the clear advantages in 1015 terms of controllability, scalability, and stimulus standard-1016 ization, several researchers are promoting the use of AI-1017 generated stimuli in psychological research (Albohn et al., 1018 2022;

1074

Across both studies, AI labelling produced consistent but 1075 small effects, driven primarily by male participants, along-1076 side robust gender differences in responses to erotic stimuli 1077 that proved sensitive to relational context. Most importantly, 1078 affective responses depended on whether participants be-1079 lieved the labels: when realism judgements were congruent 1080 with the assigned label, images labelled as photographs were 1081 rated as more arousing than those labelled as AI-generated, 1082 whereas this pattern reversed when the labels were disbe-1083 lieved. Individual differences in AI attitudes, pornography 1084 consumption, and sexual activity could not account for the la-1085 belling effect, as sensitivity to the AI label showed little reli-1086 able variability across participants. Together, these findings 1087 suggest that the anti-AI bias is best understood not as a uni-1088 form response to AI labels but as a belief-sensitive authen-1089 ticity effect, one with practical implications for researchers 1090 using synthetic stimuli and for policies mandating the disclo-1091 sure of AI-generated content. 1092 Threats, And Impact | Security Hero -securityhero.io.

Conserva-740 tive priors (𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 (0, 0.5)) will be placed again on all fixed 741 effects. 742 Marginal contrasts will be computed to compare marginal 743 means with condition (i.e., AI-generated and Photograph) 744 as the predicted contrasts, stratified by gender and congru-745 ency. The same individual-level parameter and moderator-746 correlation analyses as in Study 1 will be conducted, using 747 the same packages. To further assess the effect of the type of 748 image (e.g., couple vs individuals) the same analysis will be 749 conducted adding the type of image (image of individuals vs 750 image of couples) as predictor. 751 Consistent with Study 1, the Results section will focus on 752 Arousal as the primary outcome, highlighting where diver-753 gent trends emerge for enticement or valence; full results for 754 all outcomes are available in the analysis scripts on GitHub. 755 All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2), and all ma-756 terials, data, and analysis scripts for Study 2 are available at 757 https://github.com/RealityBending/FictionEro/tree/main/study2. same reversal pattern under incongruent trials. The primary 862 exception was for female ratings of couple images under in-863 congruent trials, where evidence remained inconclusive (pd 864 < 59.5%).

and item-level parameters showed high 868 reliability (D-vours > 0.91), very low reliability was found 869 for participant-level interactions with the AI-generated con-870 dition (D-vour = 0.072), indicating minimal reliable inter-871 individual variability in responses to the belief manipulation.

872A

similar pattern emerged for enticement and valence, al-873 though the interaction showed slightly higher (but still low) 874 reliability for valence (D-vour = 0.203).

875

Participant-specific intercepts and AI-generated param-876 eters showed only weak correlations with AI-related bias, 877 expectations, and attitudes, discrimination ability, and sex-878 ual behaviours (all |𝑟 𝑠| ≤ 0.16), with the strongest associa-879 tions observed for overall BAIT scores (𝑟 = 0.23, 95% CI 880 [0.22, 0.25]) and self-reported AI expertise (𝑟 = 0.25, 95% 881 CI [0.23, 0.27]). Similar pattern for enticement and valence 882 were found (full analysis available at the link above). Taken 883 together these findings suggest that individual variability in 884 these parameters was not meaningfully related to these con-885 structs.
